lessons.title: Two Pointers
lessons.subtitle: Two Pointers
lessons.body: Picture two people at opposite ends of a shelf of books sorted by price, looking for two books that together cost exactly your budget. If the pair is too cheap, the person at the cheap end steps inward, because even the most expensive remaining book could not lift that cheap one to the budget. If the pair is too expensive, the person at the expensive end steps inward. Each comparison rules out a whole set of pairs at once, so you never test most of the n(n-1)/2 possible pairs. In the animation, watch which cursor moves after each comparison and ask which pairs that move has ruled out. Also notice the first step: the input arrives unsorted and is sorted before the search starts, which is a separate cost.
lessons.invariant: Any pair not yet ruled out lies within the current cursor interval.
lessons.pitfall: Moving the wrong cursor. If the sum is too small and you move right inward, you throw away the partner most likely to help and can skip the answer. Too small moves left, too large moves right. On unsorted input neither move is justified, so sort first and count that cost.

blocks.title: Sort first, then two sums
blocks.text: The input arrives as 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, so the first step sorts it into 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. Now left = 0 points at 1 and right = 5 points at 7. Their sum is 8, below the target 9. Since 7 is the largest value left, no partner can rescue 1, so left moves to 1. The cursors now point at 2 and 7, the sum is 9, and the search stops with the pair 2 + 7. Only two sums were computed. Every pair containing 1 was ruled out by a single comparison, and right never had to move. The answer refers to positions in the sorted array, not to where 2 and 7 sat in the original input.

blocks.title: Why a discarded value never mattered
blocks.text: Before every comparison, any pair that sums to the target lies between left and right inclusive. It starts true because the cursors cover the whole sorted array. When the sum is too small, sorted[left] plus the largest remaining value is still short, so sorted[left] plus any smaller value is short too, and dropping left loses no answer. When the sum is too large, sorted[right] plus the smallest remaining value already overshoots, so dropping right is safe. Each step shrinks the interval by one and keeps the claim true. When left meets right, no pair of distinct positions remains, so returning false is correct.

blocks.title: Where the linear cost comes from
blocks.text: Each loop iteration either returns or moves one cursor one place inward, and the gap between them starts at n - 1. So the search makes at most n - 1 comparisons: O(n) time, with O(1) extra space for two indexes and a sum. That bound assumes the input is already sorted. If it is not, sorting costs O(n log n) and dominates; for one query on unsorted data, a hash set of values seen so far gives O(n) expected time without sorting, at the cost of O(n) space. Two pointers reports sorted positions, so keep each value's original index alongside it if the problem asks for indices. The sum is computed as a long so adding two large int values cannot overflow.

lessons.title: Binary Search
lessons.subtitle: Binary Search
lessons.body: Think of guessing a number between 1 and 100 when someone tells you higher or lower. A good guess sits in the middle, because whichever answer comes back, half of the possibilities disappear. Binary search does the same with a sorted array: one comparison with the middle value tells you which half cannot contain the target. That turns a search through n values into about log2 n comparisons, the difference between a million checks and about twenty. In the animation, keep your eye on the interval between low and high rather than on mid. Each step should shrink it, and the search ends either on a match or when the interval is empty.
lessons.invariant: If the target exists, some occurrence remains in [low,high].
lessons.pitfall: Writing low = mid or high = mid in this inclusive version. When the interval has two elements, mid equals low, so low = mid leaves the interval unchanged and the loop never ends. Test any variant on a two-element array with the target absent.

takeaways: If the target exists, it remains inside the inclusive interval [low, high]. The loop terminates when the interval becomes empty.

blocks.title: Searching for a missing 5
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is first sorted to 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, and the target is 5. The interval starts at low = 0, high = 5. The middle index is 2, holding 3. Since 3 is less than 5, the target can only be to the right, so low becomes 3. Now mid = 4 holds 6, which is too large, so high becomes 3. The interval is the single index 3, holding 4, still too small, so low becomes 4. With low = 4 and high = 3 the interval is empty, and the search returns -1. Three comparisons settled it, and the last two pinned the gap between 4 and 6, exactly where 5 would have to be.

blocks.title: The interval always holds the answer
blocks.text: If the target is in the array, some copy of it sits between low and high inclusive. At the start the interval is the whole array, so this is true. When a[mid] < target, every index up to mid holds a value no larger than a[mid], so none of them can be the target and low = mid + 1 is safe. When a[mid] > target, the same argument applies to everything from mid upward, so high = mid - 1 is safe. Because mid itself is always excluded, the interval shrinks every iteration and the loop must end. If it ends with low > high, the interval is empty, and the invariant says the target was never there.

blocks.title: Why halving gives log n
blocks.text: Each iteration removes at least half of the remaining interval, so after k steps at most n / 2^k candidates are left. The loop stops once that drops below one, which takes about log2 n iterations: O(log n) time. Space is O(1) because only low, high and mid are stored. The catch is the sorted precondition. Sorting once costs O(n log n), which pays off only when you search the same data many times; for a single lookup in unsorted data a linear scan is cheaper. Computing mid as low + (high - low) / 2 avoids int overflow on huge arrays. With duplicates, this version returns whichever match it hits first, not necessarily the first occurrence.

lessons.title: Merge Sort
lessons.subtitle: Merge Sort
lessons.body: Imagine sorting a tall stack of exam papers with a friend. You split the stack, each of you sorts half, and then you merge: look at the top paper of each sorted pile and take whichever comes first, again and again. Merge sort applies that split recursively until every pile holds one paper, which is sorted by definition. All of the real work happens in the merges. Each merge only compares the two front items, because in a sorted pile nothing behind the front can come earlier. In the animation, notice that splitting changes nothing in the array; values only move when a merge commits its buffer back. Watch the buffer fill one value at a time and count how many values each level of merging touches.
lessons.invariant: Before a merge begins, both halves are sorted. The output prefix is sorted and contains the smallest values consumed so far.
lessons.pitfall: Comparing with < instead of <= when the fronts are equal. The output is still sorted, but equal keys from the right run jump ahead of those from the left, so the sort stops being stable. Also check the two drain loops: when one run empties, the rest of the other must still be copied, or values silently disappear.

blocks.title: From pairs to the final merge
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is split at mid = 2 into indexes 0 to 2 and 3 to 5, and the left part is split again until 4 and 2 stand alone. Their merge takes 2, then 4, and the array becomes 2, 4, 7, 1, 3, 6. Merging 2, 4 with 7 takes all three in order and changes nothing. The right part repeats the pattern: 1 and 3 merge in order, then 1, 3 merges with 6, again unchanged. A merge still runs when values are already in order; the algorithm cannot know that without comparing. The final merge fills a buffer of 6 values from the fronts of 2, 4, 7 and 1, 3, 6, taking 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, then draining 7, and the array becomes 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7.

blocks.title: The buffer prefix is already final
blocks.text: During a merge, the buffer holds the smallest values consumed so far, in sorted order, and the unconsumed parts of both runs are still sorted. Each step compares only a[i] and b[j]. Every other unconsumed value sits behind one of those fronts, so it is at least as large as a front. The smaller front is therefore the smallest value left anywhere, and appending it keeps the buffer sorted. When one run empties, the rest of the other run is no smaller than anything in the buffer, so copying it in order is safe. A single value is sorted, and every merge combines two runs that smaller merges already sorted, so the top merge produces a fully sorted array.

blocks.title: Where n log n comes from
blocks.text: Halving the interval each time gives about log2 n levels of splitting. On each level the merges together touch every value once, so each level costs O(n) and the whole sort costs O(n log n). That holds for every input, sorted or reversed, which is the main reason to choose merge sort over quicksort: no bad cases. The price is the O(n) buffer each merge writes into; heapsort or quicksort sort in place instead. Taking from the left run on ties, the <= in merge, keeps equal values in their original order, so the sort is stable. For very small arrays insertion sort is often faster in practice. Merge sort also suits linked lists and data too large for memory, where sequential merging is cheap.

lessons.title: Quicksort
lessons.subtitle: Quicksort
lessons.body: Picture lining people up by height using one person as a reference. Everyone shorter or equal steps to the left, everyone taller to the right. The reference person is now standing exactly where they belong in the final line, even though neither group is sorted yet. Quicksort repeats this on each group. The step that does the work is the partition: one scan with a boundary that marks the end of the small values found so far. In the animation, watch the boundary. It advances only when a scanned value is no larger than the pivot, and a value moves only when it has to jump over a larger one. After each partition, check that the pivot never moves again.

blocks.title: Three partitions sort the row
blocks.text: With 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 the last value, 6, is the first pivot. 4 and 2 are no larger, so the boundary passes over them without moving anything. 7 is larger and stays put. Then 1 swaps with 7, giving 4, 2, 1, 7, 3, 6, and 3 swaps with 7, giving 4, 2, 1, 3, 7, 6. The pivot swaps into index 4: 4, 2, 1, 3, 6, 7. The right side holds only 7, so it is done. The left side uses pivot 3: 4 stays, 2 and then 1 swap past it, and 3 lands at index 2, giving 2, 1, 3, 4, 6, 7. Finally pivot 1 lands at index 0 and the row is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. Each partition placed its pivot for good.

blocks.title: What the boundary guarantees
blocks.text: During a partition, every value left of the boundary is no larger than the pivot, every value between the boundary and the scan position is larger, and everything past the scan is unexamined. A small value found by the scan swaps to the boundary and the boundary advances, so both regions stay correct. When the scan reaches the pivot, swapping the pivot to the boundary puts every smaller-or-equal value on its left and every larger value on its right. That is exactly its sorted position, so it never moves again. Each recursive call works on a strictly smaller range, and a range of zero or one value is already sorted, so the process ends with every value placed.

blocks.title: Why the pivot decides the cost
blocks.text: One partition scans its range once, so it costs time proportional to the range. If pivots split ranges roughly in half, there are about log n levels and each level scans about n values in total: O(n log n) on average. If the pivot is always the largest or smallest value, as a last-element pivot is on sorted input, each partition peels off one value, giving n levels and O(n²) comparisons. Recursion depth is the space cost: O(log n) on average, up to n frames in the bad case. A random pivot makes the bad case unlikely; choose merge sort when you need a guaranteed bound or stability, since quicksort is not stable. It is often fastest in practice because it sorts in place.

lessons.title: Linked Lists
lessons.subtitle: Linked Lists
lessons.body: Think of a scavenger hunt where each clue tells you where the next one is hidden. You cannot jump to the fifth clue; you have to follow the chain from the start. A singly linked list works the same way: each node stores a value and a reference to the next node, and the list is reachable only through its head. Inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is cheap, because you only rewrite references, but reaching a position is slow. Reversing the list is the classic exercise because it forces you to rewrite every arrow without losing your grip on the rest of the chain. In the animation, watch the three markers for previous, current and next, and notice that the values never move. Only the arrows change direction.

blocks.title: Six link flips, one per node
blocks.text: The chain is 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6, and previous starts as null, shown as -1. In the first step current is the node holding 4. Its next node, 2, is saved first, then the arrow from 4 is pointed at null, and the markers advance so previous is 4 and current is 2. The same three moves repeat: 2 now points back to 4, then 7 back to 2, then 1 to 7, then 3 to 1. In the sixth step current is 6, the old tail; the saved next is null, 6 is pointed at 3, and current falls off the end. previous now holds 6, which is returned as the new head, and following the arrows gives 6, 3, 1, 7, 2, 4.

blocks.title: Two lists that never overlap
blocks.text: At the top of every loop iteration the nodes form two separate lists. prev heads the part already reversed, which runs backwards from the most recent node to the original head and ends in null. current heads the untouched remainder, still linked in its original direction. No node belongs to both and none is lost. One iteration moves exactly one node from the front of the remainder to the front of the reversed part. Saving current.next before overwriting it is what keeps the remainder reachable. When current becomes null the remainder is empty, so prev heads the whole list, reversed.

blocks.text: The loop visits each node once and does a fixed amount of work there: one read and three reference writes. That gives O(n) time. A recursive reversal is shorter to write but uses one stack frame per node, O(n) space, and can overflow on long lists. Copying values into an array and writing them back also works but costs O(n) space and surprises anyone holding a reference to a particular node. Check the edges: an empty list returns null, and a one-node list returns itself. On a list with a cycle the loop never ends.

lessons.subtitle: Stacks
lessons.body: Think of a stack of plates. You add a plate to the top and take a plate from the top; the ones underneath wait until everything above them is gone. That rule, last in first out, fits every situation where the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: undo history, matching brackets, returning from nested function calls and depth-first search. A stack never lets you look inside or reorder it, and that restriction is what makes it useful, because the top always tells you what to handle next. In the animation, the values go in one order and come out in the opposite order. Notice that the first value pushed stays at the bottom until everything above it has been popped.

blocks.title: Six pushes, then six pops
blocks.text: The values 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 are pushed one at a time, and the size climbs from 1 to 6 with each new value landing on top. When the last push finishes, 6 is on top and 4 is at the bottom. Popping then removes 6 first, leaving 4, 2, 7, 1, 3. The next pops remove 3, then 1, then 7, then 2, each time taking whatever is on top. The last pop removes 4, and the stack is empty with size 0. The pop order 6, 3, 1, 7, 2, 4 is the push order reversed. Nothing was sorted or compared; the order came entirely from when each value arrived.

blocks.title: The top is the newest survivor
blocks.text: At every moment the top of the stack is the value pushed most recently among those not yet popped, and the values below it are in push order from the bottom up. A push puts the new value above the old top, which keeps that true. A pop removes the top and exposes the value pushed immediately before it, which is now the newest survivor. Because each operation touches only the top, the rest of the stack is never disturbed. That is why popping everything returns the exact reverse of the push order, and why a stack can remember where you were in nested work: the innermost open item is always on top.

blocks.title: Constant work at one end
blocks.text: Each push and pop touches only the top, so it does a fixed amount of work. ArrayDeque keeps its values in a resizable array; when the array is full it copies everything into a larger one, which is occasionally O(n) but averages out to O(1) per operation. Pushing and popping n values therefore costs O(n) time, and holding them costs O(n) space. ArrayDeque behind the Deque interface is the usual choice in Java. Check isEmpty before pop, because pop on an empty ArrayDeque throws an exception rather than returning a value. If you need the oldest item first instead of the newest, you want a queue.

lessons.body: A queue is the line at a ticket counter. People join at the back and are served from the front, so whoever has waited longest goes next. That first in, first out rule is what you want when order of arrival must be respected: print jobs, requests to a server, and the frontier in breadth-first search, where vertices must be processed in the order they were discovered. Java's ArrayDeque can act as a queue or a stack depending on which ends you use, so the discipline lives in your choice of methods, not in the container. In the animation, compare this with the stack lesson: the same six values go in, but they come out in the same order rather than reversed.

blocks.title: First in is first out
blocks.text: The values 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 are added at the back one at a time, and the size grows from 1 to 6. The front is 4 the whole time because nothing has left yet. The first removal takes 4 from the front and leaves 2, 7, 1, 3, 6. The next removals take 2, then 7, then 1, then 3, and the final one takes 6, leaving the queue empty with size 0. The removal order 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 matches the arrival order exactly. Had the same values been taken from the back instead, they would have come out reversed, which is the stack's behaviour.

blocks.title: The front waited longest
blocks.text: At every moment the front of the queue is the earliest-added value that has not been removed, and the values behind it are in arrival order. addLast puts a new value behind everything already waiting, so it cannot overtake anyone. removeFirst takes the front, which exposes the next-oldest value. Neither operation changes the relative order of the values in between. This is why breadth-first search finds fewest-edge distances: every vertex at distance d is enqueued before any vertex at distance d + 1, so the queue hands them out layer by layer.

blocks.title: Two ends, both constant time
blocks.text: ArrayDeque keeps its values in a circular array with a head index and a tail index. Adding at the back and removing from the front each move one index, so they cost O(1); when the array fills, it is copied into a larger one, which averages out to O(1) per operation. Processing n values therefore takes O(n) time and up to O(n) space while they wait. An ArrayList used as a queue is a common slow alternative, because removing index 0 shifts every remaining element and makes each removal O(n). If items should leave by priority rather than arrival, use a priority queue. Check isEmpty before removeFirst, which throws on an empty deque.

lessons.title: Recursion and the Call Stack
lessons.subtitle: Recursion and the Call Stack
lessons.body: Picture a line of people passing a question along: each person asks the next one an easier version and waits, notes in hand, until the answer comes back. The last person can answer without asking anyone. Then the answers travel back, and each person finishes their own part using the answer they received. A recursive function works this way. Each call gets its own frame on the call stack, holding its own copy of n, and stays paused until the smaller call returns. Every recursive function needs a base case that answers directly and a call that moves toward it. In the animation, the column of frames is the call stack. Notice that it grows first with no multiplying at all, and every multiplication happens while the stack shrinks.

lessons.pitfall: A missing base case or a call that does not reduce the problem can recurse indefinitely. The call stack consumes space even when no explicit array is allocated.

blocks.title: Five frames wait for the base case
blocks.text: The animation computes factorial(5). The first call cannot answer yet, so it pauses and calls factorial(4), which pauses and calls factorial(3), and so on. After five calls the stack holds frames for 5, 4, 3, 2 and 1, and the call for 0 is pushed on top. That call hits the base case and returns 1 without recursing. Its frame is popped, and the frame for 1 resumes: 1 times 1 is 1. Each paused frame then resumes in turn, newest first: 2 times 1 gives 2, 3 times 2 gives 6, 4 times 6 gives 24, and 5 times 24 gives 120. The stack is empty again and the result is 120.

blocks.title: Each frame trusts the smaller call
blocks.text: factorial(n) returns n times factorial(n - 1), and factorial(0) returns 1. To see that every call returns the right answer, argue by induction on n. The base case is correct by definition. If factorial(n - 1) returns (n - 1)!, then n times it is n!, so factorial(n) is correct too. Termination comes from the argument shrinking by one each call, so it must reach 0. While a call is paused, its local n is safe in its own frame; the smaller calls get their own frames and cannot overwrite it. That is why the frame for 5 still multiplies by 5 after four deeper calls have come and gone.

blocks.title: Paying for the waiting frames
blocks.text: factorial(n) makes n + 1 calls, each doing one comparison and at most one multiplication, so the time is O(n). The space is also O(n), not because of any array but because up to n + 1 frames are alive at once on the call stack. That stack is limited, and very deep recursion crashes with a stack overflow. A loop that multiplies 1 through n gives the same answer in O(1) space, and Java does not optimise tail calls, so for a simple linear recursion like this a loop is the safer choice. Recursion pays off when the problem branches, as in trees and backtracking. The Java rejects negative n, which has no base case to reach, and caps n at 10 to keep the example small.

lessons.title: Backtracking
lessons.subtitle: Backtracking
lessons.body: Imagine exploring a maze with a ball of string. At each fork you pick a corridor and keep unrolling string. When a corridor ends, you wind the string back to the last fork and try the next corridor. You never need a second ball of string, because winding back restores exactly where you were. Backtracking explores every combination of choices the same way: one shared path list, an add before exploring a branch and a remove after it. Generating all subsets is the cleanest example, since each value is either in or out. In the animation, watch the path grow and shrink like the string. Every undo should restore the path to exactly what it was before the matching choice, and every recorded subset is a copy, not the live path.

blocks.title: Following the path through the trace
blocks.text: The trace begins by recording the empty path. It then chooses values in input order and records each path on the way down: 4, then 4, 2, then 4, 2, 7, then 4, 2, 7, 1, then 4, 2, 7, 1, 3. Nothing is left to add, so it undoes 3 and then 1, returning to 4, 2, 7, and records 4, 2, 7, 3. Undoing 3 and 7 brings it back to 4, 2, which leads to 4, 2, 1, then 4, 2, 1, 3, then 4, 2, 3. Removing 2 leaves 4, and the next branch is 4, 7. A long stretch continues the same way. Near the end the path visits 7, 3, then 1 and 1, 3, then 3 alone, and the final undo leaves it empty. This trace uses only the first five values, so 6 never joins the path.

blocks.title: Undo restores the parent exactly
blocks.text: Whenever a call starts, the shared path holds exactly the choices made on the way from the root of the decision tree to this call, and nothing else. Each call that adds a value removes that same value before it returns, so the path is handed back to its caller unchanged. That is what lets siblings share one list: the second branch starts from the same path the first branch started from. In the Java, visit(i) is entered with path holding the chosen values among indices below i, so when i reaches a.length the path is one complete subset and a copy goes into out. Each subset matches one root-to-leaf route, so none is missed or repeated.

blocks.title: Exponential output, linear working space
blocks.text: With n distinct values there are 2^n subsets, because each value is independently in or out. lessons.body: A family tree has a person at the top and branches below, and there is no single obvious order to read it in. Tree traversal gives you rules for that order. Preorder visits the node first, inorder in the middle, postorder last. Inorder matters most for binary search trees, where it reads values in sorted order, but the rule itself knows nothing about values; it only follows links. blocks.title: Left, node, right on this tree
blocks.text: The input 4, 2, 7, 1, 3, 6 is read as level-order slots: 4 is the root, 2 and 7 are its children, 1 and 3 hang under 2, and 6 is the left child of 7. The walk enters 4, then 2, then 1. Node 1 has no left child, so it emits 1 and returns. Back in 2, the left side is done, so it emits 2, then enters 3, emits 3 and returns. Node 2 returns to 4, which emits 4 and turns right. It enters 7, then 6, emits 6 and returns. Node 7 emits 7, has no right child, and returns, and finally 4 returns. The output is 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7. It is sorted because this tree happens to satisfy the search-tree ordering, not because inorder sorts anything.

blocks.title: A subtree finishes before moving on
blocks.text: When walk returns from a node, out has gained exactly the values of that node's subtree, in inorder, and nothing else. For an empty subtree this holds trivially, because walk returns at once. For a real node, the first recursive call adds its whole left subtree in order, then out.add places the node, then the second call adds the right subtree. Each subtree is smaller, so the claim follows by induction from the leaves up, and calling walk on the root lists every node exactly once. The order depends only on the shape of the links. If the tree also has the search-tree property, that order is sorted.

blocks.title: Linear time, height-deep stack
blocks.text: walk is called once for each node and once for each null child, and a tree with n nodes has n + 1 null links, so there are 2n + 1 calls doing constant work each: O(n) time. The space that matters is the call stack, which holds one frame per node on the current root-to-leaf path, so O(h) where h is the height. For a balanced tree h is about log n; for a tree that degenerates into a chain h is n, and a deep enough chain can overflow the stack. An explicit stack in a loop avoids that limit, and level order needs a queue instead. The output list adds O(n). height uses the same pattern and counts nodes, so the empty tree has height 0.

lessons.subtitle: Heaps and Priority Queues
lessons.body: Think of a company org chart where every manager earns more than the people who report directly to them. You can see the top earner at a glance, but nothing tells you whether someone in one department earns more than someone in another. A max-heap keeps exactly that weak order: every parent is at least as large as its children, so the maximum is always at the root. Because the tree is complete, it packs into an array with no gaps. That partial order is cheaper to maintain than full sorting, which is why heaps power priority queues. In the animation, follow the newly inserted value. It only ever moves up its own path toward the root, and it stops at the first parent that is at least as large.

blocks.title: Six insertions, three swaps
blocks.text: Inserting 4 makes it the root. 2 lands at index 1; its parent at index 0 holds 4, which is larger, so nothing moves. 7 lands at index 2, its parent 4 is smaller, so they swap and the array is 7, 2, 4 with 7 at the root. 1 lands at index 3 under 2 and stays. 3 lands at index 4, beats its parent 2 at index 1 and swaps up, giving 7, 3, 4, 1, 2; the next comparison with 7 stops it. Finally 6 lands at index 5, beats its parent 4 at index 2 and swaps, giving 7, 3, 6, 1, 2, 4, and 7 stops it again. The root is the maximum, but the array is not sorted in either direction.

blocks.title: Only one path can break
blocks.text: Before each insertion, every parent in the array is at least as large as its children. Adding a value at the end can break that rule in one place only: between the new value and its parent. If the parent is at least as large, the heap is valid and the loop breaks. If not, swapping fixes that pair, and the value that moves down was already the parent of that position, so it is still at least as large as anything below it. The only possible violation has moved one level up the same path. Repeating this ends at a large-enough parent or at index 0, and either way the whole array is a valid heap again, with the maximum at the root.

blocks.title: Height bounds every insertion
blocks.text: A complete tree with n nodes has height about log2 n, and an inserted value climbs at most that many levels, comparing and maybe swapping once per level. So one insertion costs O(log n), and inserting n values one by one costs O(n log n). The array holds every value once, O(n) space, with no child references because index arithmetic replaces them. Use a heap when you repeatedly need the current maximum while values keep arriving. If you need everything in order once, sort instead; searching a heap for an arbitrary value is O(n). Building a heap bottom-up from a full array is O(n), faster than repeated insertion. Equal values are fine: the >= check stops the climb.

lessons.title: Depth-First Search
lessons.subtitle: Depth-First Search
lessons.body: Picture exploring a cave with a ball of string. You follow one passage as far as it goes, and only when it dead-ends do you wind the string back to the last fork and try the next opening. Depth-first search does the same on a graph: the call stack is the string, recording the path from the start to where you stand. It answers questions such as which vertices can I reach, is there a cycle, or what belongs to one connected piece. In the animation, watch the list of open frames grow by one vertex each time the search goes deeper, and shrink by one each time a vertex is finished. The order in which vertices are entered and the order in which they finish are both useful later, for example in topological sorting.

lessons.pitfall: Do not expect DFS to find shortest routes. It follows the first neighbour as deep as it goes, so a target one edge away can be reached through a long detour first. Also mark a vertex when you enter it, not when you finish it. If the mark comes late, a cycle sends the search back into a vertex that is still on the path, and the recursion never ends.

blocks.title: One long dive, then unwind
blocks.text: The search starts at vertex 0 and marks it entered. From 0 it descends to neighbour 1 before looking at any other neighbour of 0, and the same thing repeats: 1 descends to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4, and 4 to 5. At that moment six frames are open, [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5], which is the exact path from the source. Vertex 5 has nothing new to explore, so it finishes and returns. Then 4, 3, 2, 1 and 0 finish in turn. None of them finds another unvisited neighbour on the way back, so the stack empties without a second dive. The final state reports 6 visited vertices, and the entry order 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 is what dfs returns in its out list.

blocks.title: The open frames are the path
blocks.text: At every moment, the open frames form a path of discovered vertices from the source to the vertex being explored, and each of them may still have neighbours left to check. A vertex is marked in seen the moment explore is called on it, before any of its neighbours are tried. That early mark keeps the search finite: if a cycle leads back to a vertex already marked, the check fails and the search does not enter it again. When a frame returns, every vertex reachable from it through still-unmarked vertices has been entered. So no vertex is entered twice, and every vertex reachable from the source is entered once.

blocks.title: Each edge is checked once
blocks.text: Each vertex is entered once because seen blocks a second entry, and each vertex's neighbour list is scanned once while its frame is open. Across the whole graph that is V entries plus E neighbour checks, so the time is O(V+E) with adjacency lists. The space is O(V): the seen array has one slot per vertex, and in the worst case, a long chain like the one in this trace, the call stack holds every vertex at once. On a large graph shaped like a long line, recursion can overflow Java's stack, so switch to an explicit stack. If you need the fewest edges to a target, use BFS instead. The outer loop in dfs restarts from every unmarked vertex, so disconnected parts are covered too.

lessons.body: Suppose a friend asks you for 37 times 43 and you work it out on paper. If they ask again five minutes later, you read your answer off the paper instead of redoing the multiplication. Memoization gives a recursive function that same notepad. Plain recursive Fibonacci calls F(n-1) and F(n-2), and those two calls share almost all of their work, so the number of calls explodes as n grows. Storing each answer the first time it is finished collapses that tree of calls into one computation per value of n. In the animation, watch two things: the chain of frames that dives down to the base cases once, and the cache hits on the way back up, where a call returns at once without opening any deeper frames.

If the two recursive calls still run on every visit and memo is only written afterwards, the table fills up but nothing is saved. A quick test: every repeated n should show a cache hit with no new frames under it. Also keep not computed apart from a computed zero; memo uses Integer and null for that reason.

blocks.title: Dive once, then reuse
blocks.text: The trace computes F(8). The first call opens frames for 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and finally 1, always taking the n minus one branch first. F(1) returns 1 and F(0) returns 0 as base cases, so F(2) is stored as 1. Back in F(3), its second call F(1) is another base case, and F(3) is stored as 2. Now the reuse starts. F(4) needs F(2), which is already in the table: a cache hit returns 1 with no new frames, and F(4) is stored as 3. The same pattern repeats at every level. F(5) reuses F(3) and becomes 5, F(6) reuses F(4) and becomes 8, F(7) reuses F(5) and becomes 13, and F(8) reuses F(6) and becomes 21. The finished table is [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21], and the answer read from it is 21.

blocks.title: A stored value is final
blocks.text: Once memo holds a value for n, that value is the true F(n) and never changes. It is written only after both recursive calls have returned, and those calls return correct values by the same argument applied to smaller n, with F(0) and F(1) returned directly as base cases. So a cache hit is safe: reading memo[n] gives exactly what recomputing would give. The table in the trace fills strictly left to right, because an entry can only be written after the entries it depends on. The bottom-up fibTable relies on the same fact in loop form: when it writes dp[i], the two entries before it are already final.

blocks.title: Calls drop from exponential to linear
blocks.text: Without the cache, F(n) makes two calls that each make two more, and the shared work is redone again and again, so the call count grows exponentially, roughly like the Fibonacci numbers themselves. With memo, each n from 2 up to the target is computed once, and every other call is a base case or a cache hit that does constant work. That gives O(n) time. Space is O(n) for the memo array, plus O(n) for the recursion stack, which in the trace is deepest with 8 frames open. fibTable has the same O(n) time and table with no recursion, so it cannot overflow the stack. If you only need the final value, keep the last two numbers and the space drops to O(1). Note that int overflows after F(46); use long for larger n.

blocks.title: Three counters for n = 8
blocks.text: With n = 8, the scan loop visits positions 0 through 7, and its counter climbs one step at a time until it reads 8. The nested loop counts ordered pairs. Each outer row contributes a full inner loop of 8 visits, so the counter jumps to 8, 16, 24, 32, 40, 48, 56 and ends at 64 after row 7. The halving loop starts with x at 8 and divides by two: it visits 8, 4, 2 and 1, and when x becomes 0 the loop stops, giving 4 visits. The final comparison is 8, 64 and 4 for the same input size. Try predicting n = 16 before you run it: the scan doubles, the pair count grows fourfold, and the halving count grows by one.

blocks.title: Count what the body does
blocks.text: Each counter in counts goes up by exactly one every time its loop body runs, so when a loop finishes, its counter equals the number of times that body executed. That is the whole method: choose the operation you care about, write down how many times it runs, and keep the term that grows fastest. For the scan the count is n. For the square loop the inner body runs n times for each of n outer values, so n times n. For halving, x takes the values n, n/2, n/4 and so on down to 1, which is about log2(n) plus one values. Big-O then drops constant factors and smaller terms, because they stop mattering as n grows.

blocks.title: Why growth beats milliseconds
blocks.text: The three loops cost O(n), O(n²) and O(log n) time because those are the formulas their counters follow. Space is O(1) auxiliary: however large n is, counts keeps three long counters and a loop variable or two, and nothing grows with n. Growth rate matters more than constant factors once inputs get large. At n = 1000 the scan does a thousand visits and the square loop a million, so a quadratic method that was fine on a small test can stall on real data. Counting has limits too. It ignores memory effects and fixed overhead, so for small n a plain O(n²) loop can beat a cleverer method. Treat Big-O as a guide to how cost scales, then measure when the constants matter.

lessons.body: Think of an array as a row of numbered lockers. Each locker has a fixed position, and you can open locker 2 directly without walking past lockers 0 and 1. That direct jump is why arrays are the default container for ordered data: reading or writing any slot by its index costs the same, however long the row is. The index names a place, not what is stored there, so two lockers can hold the same value and still be different slots. blocks.title: Summing [2, 1, 5] slot by slot
blocks.text: Before the loop starts, total is 0 because nothing has been read yet. At index 0 the loop reads 2, and total becomes 2. At index 1 it reads 1, and total becomes 3. At index 2 it reads 5, and total becomes 8. The condition i < a.length now fails, since the length is 3, and sum returns 8. Notice that each step adds only the value in the current slot. The earlier slots are never read again, because total already stands for them. If the array were empty, the loop body would never run and the method would return the starting value 0.

blocks.title: Total covers the slots behind i
blocks.text: Each time the loop is about to read index i, total equals the sum of every slot before i and none after it. At the start i is 0 and no slots are behind it, so total must be 0, which is how it is initialised. Each iteration adds a[i] and then moves i forward by one, so the statement is true again for the new i. When the loop ends, i equals a.length, and every slot before i means the whole array. That is why the returned value is the full sum. This style of reasoning, true at the start, kept by each step, useful at the end, is how you check any loop.

blocks.title: One visit per slot
blocks.text: The loop body runs once per slot and does constant work each time, so summing takes O(n) time. You cannot do better for a sum, because every value must be read at least once. Auxiliary space is O(1): one long and one int index, whatever the length. The accumulator is long rather than int because adding many large ints can pass the int limit of about 2.1 billion and wrap silently to a negative number. Arrays are the right tool for indexed reads and scans, but their size is fixed when they are created, and inserting into the middle means shifting every later slot. When the size changes often, a growable list or a linked structure fits better.

blocks.title: Reversing "cat" into a buffer
blocks.text: The source is "cat", with c at index 0, a at index 1 and t at index 2. The output buffer starts empty. The loop begins at the last index, 2, and appends t, so the output is "t". Next it reads index 1 and appends a, giving "ta". Then it reads index 0 and appends c, giving "tac". The index would now be negative, the condition i >= 0 fails, and reverse returns "tac". The source is still "cat", because every step only read from it. Notice that the read index goes 2, 1, 0 while the output length goes 1, 2, 3. That is why the two must be tracked separately.

blocks.title: The buffer holds a reversed suffix
blocks.text: After k characters have been appended, the buffer holds the last k characters of the source in reverse order. Before the loop, k is 0 and the buffer is empty, which matches. Each step reads the next character further left and appends it to the right end of the buffer, so the reversed suffix grows by one and stays in the right order. When i passes index 0, k equals the length of the source, the suffix is the whole string, and the buffer is its full reverse. Because nothing is ever written to s, any other code holding a reference to it still sees the original text.

blocks.title: Why the builder keeps it linear
blocks.text: The loop runs once per character, and each append adds one character to the end of the builder, which is amortised constant work. So the reversal costs O(n) time. Space is O(n) because the output is a new string of the same length, which you cannot avoid since the original cannot be changed. Concatenating onto a String with + inside the loop would copy the partial result on every step, 1 + 2 + ... + n characters in total, which is O(n²). For one or two concatenations + is fine. One caution: charAt reads UTF-16 code units, so reversing text with emoji or combined accents can split a character in two.

lessons.body: Think of a coat check. You hand over a coat, get a ticket number, and later the attendant goes straight to the right hook instead of searching every coat. A hash set does that for values: it turns a key into a bucket number, goes to that bucket, and compares only the few keys stored there. A hash map adds a value to each key, such as a count or an earlier index. This turns questions like have I seen this before, or how many times did this appear, from a scan of everything seen so far into one lookup that takes expected constant time. In the animation, notice that two different keys can land in the same bucket. The bucket only narrows the search; an equality check decides whether the key is really there.

blocks.title: Counting [2, 1, 6, 2, 5]
blocks.text: The trace follows frequencies on [2, 1, 6, 2, 5], using an illustrative bucket rule of key mod 4. Key 2 goes to bucket 2, is not found, and enters with count 1. Key 1 goes to bucket 1 and enters with count 1. Key 6 also lands in bucket 2, but equality shows it is not 2, so it becomes a separate entry: 3 unique keys now. The second 2 goes to bucket 2, matches the existing key, and its count rises to 2 without a new entry. Finally 5 shares bucket 1 with key 1 and enters as the fourth unique key. The map ends with 2 counted twice and 1, 6 and 5 once each. With duplicate, the second 2 is where seen.add returns false and the method returns true.

blocks.title: The table mirrors what came before
blocks.text: Before position i is read, the set or map contains exactly the distinct values from positions before i, and in frequencies each count equals how often that value has appeared so far. It starts empty, which is correct for an empty prefix. Each step either finds the key and updates it, or inserts it, so the statement holds again for the next position. For duplicate this gives a clean proof: seen.add fails exactly when the current value already appeared earlier, so the first false means a repeat, and finishing the loop means every value was new. Correctness also rests on equality and hashing agreeing: equal keys must hash to the same bucket, or a lookup searches the wrong place.

blocks.title: Expected constant, not guaranteed
blocks.text: Each element costs one lookup plus one insert or update. With a good hash function and a table that resizes as it fills, buckets stay short, so each operation takes expected constant time and the whole pass is expected O(n). The worst case is worse: if many keys collide, a bucket grows long and lookups slow down, which is why the bound says expected. Space is O(n) because, when all values are distinct, every one gets an entry. Compare the alternatives. Checking each value against all earlier ones is O(n²) with no extra memory, and sorting first is O(n log n) and puts repeats next to each other. Use a LinkedHashMap, as frequencies does, when you also need the insertion order back.

blocks.title: Building [0, 2, 3, 8]
blocks.text: The input is [2, 1, 5]. Boundary 0 stores 0, since nothing has been added yet. Boundary 1 stores 0 + 2 = 2, the sum of the first value. Boundary 2 stores 2 + 1 = 3. Boundary 3 stores 3 + 5 = 8, the sum of the whole array. The table has 4 entries for 3 values, one per boundary. The query asks for the half-open range from 1 to 3, which covers the values 1 and 5. The method reads the entry at the right boundary, 8, and subtracts the entry at the left boundary, 2, giving 6. Check by hand: 1 + 5 is 6.

blocks.title: Each entry sums everything before it
blocks.text: p[i] always equals the sum of the first i values of a, and p[0] is 0 because zero values add to nothing. The loop keeps this true: p[i + 1] is p[i] plus a[i], so it covers exactly one more value. Given that, a range from left to right, including left and excluding right, is the first right values with the first left values taken away. That is p[right] minus p[left], and nothing else is needed. The half-open convention is what keeps the formula clean: the range length is right minus left, and an empty range, where left equals right, correctly sums to 0.

blocks.title: One pass now, constant time later
blocks.text: Building the table touches each value once, so it costs O(n) time, and the table takes O(n) space for its n plus one entries. Each range query then reads two entries and subtracts, which is O(1) however wide the range is. For a single query this is no win, since summing the range directly is also O(n). The payoff comes with many queries: q questions cost O(n + q) instead of up to O(n times q). Prefix sums work with negative values too. They handle updates badly: changing one value forces every later entry to change, so for frequent updates use a Fenwick tree or a segment tree. The entries are long so that sums of many values do not overflow.

blocks.title: Why "abba" needs a loop
blocks.text: Take "abba". With right at 0 the frame is a and best becomes 1. With right at 1 the frame is ab and best becomes 2. At right 2 the incoming b is already inside. Removing the leftmost character, a, moves left to 1, but the old b is still there, so shrinking continues: removing b moves left to 2. Now the frame is the single b at index 2 and best stays 2. At right 3 the incoming a is no longer in the set, because it left during the shrink, so the frame becomes ba from index 2 to 3, length 2. The answer is best = 2. A single if in place of the while would have stopped after removing a and left two b characters in the frame.

blocks.title: Distinct after every shrink
blocks.text: After the while loop ends and incoming is added, window holds exactly the characters from index left through index right, all distinct. The loop runs until incoming is absent, so adding it cannot create a repeat. Why is it safe to drop characters from the left for good? Any frame that starts before the new left and ends at right would contain the repeated character twice, and extending such a frame further right keeps that repeat. So no frame the method skips can be valid and longer than one it measured, and best ends as the true maximum.

blocks.title: Each character enters and leaves once
blocks.text: The right edge moves n times in total, and the left edge moves at most n times across the whole run, since it never moves back. Each move does one set operation in expected constant time, so the total is expected O(n), even though there is a loop inside a loop. Space is O(min(n, alphabet size)) because the set holds only distinct characters: at most the length of the string, and at most the size of the alphabet. A brute-force check of every substring costs O(n²) or more. Use this pattern only when shrinking from the left always helps restore validity. For sums with negative numbers that property fails, and prefix sums with a hash map are the usual alternative.

lessons.body: Picture bookings for a shared meeting room, written as time ranges on a whiteboard in no particular order. To see when the room is actually busy, you would first line the bookings up by start time, then sweep left to right, joining any booking that starts before the current busy block ends. That is interval merging. Sorting is the step that makes it work: once starts are in order, a new interval can only overlap the most recent merged block, so you never look further back. The same sort-then-sweep idea shows up in calendar conflicts and total covered length. In the animation, notice that each interval causes exactly one of two outcomes: extend the last block, or start a new one.
lessons.invariant: Output segments are disjoint and cover exactly the processed input intervals.
lessons.pitfall: For closed intervals [1,2] and [2,3], equality means overlap. Half-open intervals need a different convention. Never mutate caller intervals accidentally while merging.

checkpoint.explanation: Both contain 2, so the merged interval is [1,3].

blocks.title: Merging three segments
blocks.text: The input pairs are [1, 3], [2, 6] and [8, 10], so there are 3 intervals. Sorting by start leaves them in the same order, since 1, 2, 8 is already ascending. The output is empty, so [1, 3] is appended and there is 1 merged block. Next, [2, 6] starts at 2, which is not past the block's end of 3, so the two overlap and the block's end grows to the larger end, 6. The count stays at 1 and the block is now [1, 6]. Finally [8, 10] starts at 8, past the end 6, so it is appended as a separate block. The result is [1, 6] and [8, 10]: 2 blocks.

blocks.title: Only the last block can overlap
blocks.text: After each interval is processed, the output blocks are in order, do not overlap, and together cover exactly the intervals seen so far. Sorting is what lets the loop compare only with the last block. Every earlier block ends before the last block starts, and every new interval starts at or after the last block's start, so a new interval cannot reach back to an earlier block. If the new start is at most the last end, the two share at least one point and joining them keeps coverage exact. If the start is greater, there is a real gap, and a new block keeps the output disjoint. Taking the larger of the two ends matters when one interval sits inside another.

blocks.title: Sorting dominates the cost
blocks.text: The sweep visits each interval once and does constant work, so it is O(n). The sort before it is O(n log n), and that term dominates, so the whole method is O(n log n). If the intervals already arrive sorted by start, you can skip the sort and merge in O(n). Space is O(n): mergeIntervals clones every pair so the caller's arrays are not changed, and the output can hold up to n blocks when nothing overlaps. Decide edge cases up front. Touching endpoints such as [1, 2] and [2, 3] merge here because the intervals are closed, while half-open ranges would keep them apart. An empty input returns an empty array.

lessons.body: A matrix is a grid, like a spreadsheet or a seating chart. Every cell has two coordinates: which row it is in and which column. In Java a matrix is an array of row arrays, so a[r][c] means pick row r first, then column c inside it. Grids appear everywhere: images, game boards, distance tables, and the adjacency matrix of a graph. The transpose is a good first exercise because it forces you to keep the two dimensions apart. Rows become columns, so a wide grid turns tall. In the animation, follow one source cell to its new home and notice that its two coordinates trade places, while the row and column counts of the output trade places too.

blocks.title: From 2 × 3 to 3 × 2
blocks.text: The input values 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 form 2 rows of 3: row 0 is 1, 2, 3 and row 1 is 4, 5, 6. So out is created with 3 rows and 2 columns. The loop walks the source row by row. Cell (0,0) goes to (0,0), (0,1) goes to (1,0) and (0,2) goes to (2,0). The first source row becomes the first output column, which now reads 1, 2, 3 from top to bottom. Then (1,0) goes to (0,1), (1,1) to (1,1) and (1,2) to (2,1), filling column 1 with 4, 5, 6. The result is [[1, 4], [2, 5], [3, 6]]. Cells on the diagonal, (0,0) and (1,1), keep their coordinates.

blocks.title: Cell (r, c) lands at (c, r)
blocks.text: Every source cell a[r][c] is written to out[c][r], and each output cell receives exactly one source cell. That one rule makes the whole result correct: row r of the input becomes column r of the output, and column c becomes row c. The output shape follows from it. Source row numbers now index output columns, so out needs cols rows and rows columns. The nested loop visits every (r, c) pair once, so no cell is missed or copied twice. The ragged check before the loop guarantees that a[r][c] exists for every r and c the loop will touch.

blocks.title: Every cell is copied once
blocks.text: The nested loop runs cols times for each of rows, and each pass copies one value, so the time is O(rows × columns). You cannot do better, because every cell must move. Space is also O(rows × columns), since the result is a new grid with the same number of cells. A square matrix can be transposed in place by swapping a[r][c] with a[c][r] for the cells above the diagonal, which needs O(1) extra space, but a non-square grid cannot, because its shape changes. Edge cases: zero rows give an empty result, and a ragged input, where rows have different lengths, is rejected with an exception instead of producing a wrong grid.

lessons.body: A graph is a set of things and the connections between them: cities and roads, people and friendships, web pages and links. The things are vertices and the connections are edges. Before any search can run, you need to store the connections so that you can quickly ask what is next to this vertex. An adjacency list gives each vertex its own row listing where its edges lead. It is like one contacts page per person: you open a page and see only that person's links, not the whole network. In the animation, watch the rows get created first, one per vertex even if nothing connects to it, and then watch each edge drop its endpoint into the row of the vertex it leaves from.

blocks.title: Four rows, three edges
blocks.text: The trace uses 4 vertices and the edges 0 to 1, 0 to 2 and 2 to 3. First, adjacency creates 4 empty rows, numbered 0 to 3, before reading any edge, so a vertex with no edges still has a row. Edge 0 to 1 adds 1 to row 0. Edge 0 to 2 adds 2 to row 0, which now reads [1, 2]. Edge 2 to 3 adds 3 to row 2. After 3 edges the graph is [[1, 2], [], [3], []]. Rows 1 and 3 stay empty: those vertices have no outgoing edges, even though edges point into them. Because the edges are directed, asking for the neighbours of 1 returns nothing, not 0.

blocks.title: Each edge lands in one row
blocks.text: Every edge u to v that has been read appears as v in row u, once, and nowhere else. The rows are created for all n vertices before any edge is read, so every valid u has a row waiting. The validity check rejects an edge whose endpoint is outside 0 to n minus one, so a bad edge cannot slip into the wrong row or cause a crash later. With this property, the neighbours of u are exactly row u, which is what BFS and DFS rely on. For an undirected graph, add each edge twice, u to v and v to u. Repeated edges and self loops are kept as given, so decide whether your problem allows them.

blocks.title: Lists versus a matrix
blocks.text: Building takes O(V+E) time: one pass creates V rows and a second pass appends each of the E edges in amortised constant time. Space is O(V+E) for the same reason, one row per vertex plus one entry per edge. An adjacency matrix uses V × V cells, so it costs O(V²) space even when there are few edges, but it answers whether an edge u to v exists in O(1). Lists are the usual choice for sparse graphs, where E is far smaller than V², and they let you loop over a vertex's neighbours in time proportional to how many it has. When vertex names are strings rather than 0 to n minus one, map each name to an index first with a hash map.

problems.description: Count readings equal to zero.
problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Walk through the readings once, keeping a counter of how many equal zero. The invariant is simple: after looking at the first i readings, the counter holds exactly the number of zeros among them, so after the last reading it holds the answer. Each reading is inspected once, so the time is O(n) and, apart from storing the input, the extra space is O(1). There is nothing to sort or remember. Edge cases: a sequence with no zeros at all prints 0 (not an empty line), a single reading of 0 prints 1, and a run where every reading is zero prints n. Negative readings are never zero, however close to it.
hints: Only one property of each reading matters here: whether it is exactly zero. Its sign and size are irrelevant.
Keep a single running counter. Each reading either adds one to it or leaves it unchanged.
Scan the readings once and increment the counter on every value equal to 0. Negative numbers are not zero, and a line with no zeros must still print 0.

problems.editorial: Read every token, then output them from the last index down to the first. This is the stack idea in its simplest form: the first item in is the last item out. Correctness is direct, since position i of the output holds input position n-1-i, which is exactly the reversed order. The tokens never need to be parsed as numbers because reversing does not depend on their values, so printing them unchanged keeps signs such as -10000 intact. Time is O(n) for one pass and space is O(n) for the stored list (an in-place two-pointer swap would also work). Edge cases: a single reading prints itself, repeated values stay in their mirrored positions, and the output has no trailing separator.
hints: There is no leading count: every token on the input line is a reading, so read the whole input and split it on whitespace.
The last reading must be printed first. A stack does exactly this: push in input order, pop in reverse order. Walking an array backwards is the same idea.
Iterate the index from the last position down to 0 and join the values with single spaces. A single reading is its own reverse, and negative values must keep their minus sign.

problems.editorial: Read every token, convert it to an integer and sort the list with the language's built-in sort, then print it separated by single spaces. The built-in sort is a comparison sort, so after it finishes every adjacent pair satisfies a[i] <= a[i+1], which is exactly the nondecreasing order requested. It runs in O(n log n) time and O(n) space. A hand-written insertion sort (O(n^2)) would also pass for n <= 1000, and because values lie in [-10000, 10000] a counting sort over 20001 buckets would run in linear time. Edge cases: a single value, many duplicates, and negative numbers, which must be compared numerically rather than as strings.

problems.title: Out-of-order pairs
problems.description: Count pairs i < j for which a[i] > a[j].
problems.constraints: One nonempty line of 1–1000 integers, each between -10000 and 10000.
problems.inputFormat: Read the sequence until end of input; there is no leading length.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: This is inversion counting. The direct approach checks every pair in O(n^2), which is fine for 1000 values but does not scale. Merge sort counts inversions in O(n log n): split the array, count inversions inside each half recursively, then count pairs that cross the halves while merging. Because both halves are sorted, whenever the right head is strictly smaller than the left head it is also smaller than all remaining left values, so all of them form inversions with it. Taking the left value on ties keeps equal pairs uncounted. Space is O(n) for the merge buffers. Edge cases: one value or sorted input gives 0, strictly decreasing input gives n(n-1)/2, and duplicates contribute nothing.
hints: Only strictly greater counts: equal values at positions i < j do not form an out-of-order pair.
Merge sort can count these pairs. While merging two sorted halves, a value taken from the right half is smaller than every value still waiting in the left half.
When the right value is strictly smaller, add the number of remaining left values to the count; on a tie take the left value first so equal pairs are never counted.

references.python:
import sys


def sort_and_count(a):
    """Return (sorted copy of a, number of pairs i < j with a[i] > a[j])."""
    if len(a) <= 1:
        return a, 0
    mid = len(a) // 2
    left, left_count = sort_and_count(a[:mid])
    right, right_count = sort_and_count(a[mid:])
    merged = []
    count = left_count + right_count
    i = j = 0
    while i < len(left) and j < len(right):
        if left[i] <= right[j]:
            merged.append(left[i])
            i += 1
        else:
            # right[j] is smaller than every remaining left value
            count += len(left) - i
            merged.append(right[j])
            j += 1
    merged.extend(left[i:])
    merged.extend(right[j:])
    return merged, count


values = [int(x) for x in sys.stdin.read().split()]
print(sort_and_count(values)[1])

problems.editorial: Count occurrences of every value in a hash map, then look for a value whose count is greater than n // 2. Counting takes O(n) expected time and O(k) space for k distinct values. problems.editorial: This is the stock-span problem solved with a monotonic stack. For each index i, the span is i - p where p is the closest earlier index with a value strictly greater than a[i] (or -1 if there is none). Keep a stack of indices with strictly decreasing values. Before pushing i, pop every index whose value is <= a[i]: those values are covered by a[i] and can never be the blocker for anything later. Whatever is left on top is p. Each index is pushed and popped at most once, so the total time is O(n) with O(n) space, versus O(n^2) for scanning backwards from every position. Keep a stack of indices whose values are strictly decreasing; anything smaller or equal to the current value can never block a later span, so it can be thrown away.

import sys

values = [int(token) for token in sys.stdin.read().split()]
stack = []  # indices whose values are strictly decreasing from bottom to top
spans = []

    previous_greater = stack[-1] if stack else -1
    spans.append(i - previous_greater)
    stack.append(i)
print(' '.join(str(s) for s in spans))

problems.title: Bits switched on

problems.constraints: One integer within the range stated above.

problems.editorial: Use Kernighan's trick. Subtracting 1 from n flips its lowest set bit to 0 and every zero below it to 1, so n & (n - 1) is n with that lowest set bit removed and everything else unchanged. Repeating until n is 0 removes one set bit per step, so the number of steps is the answer. The loop runs once per set bit, at most 5 times for n <= 30, with O(1) space. The simpler baseline checks n & 1 and shifts right, which costs one step per bit position instead of per set bit. Edge cases: n = 0 (the loop never runs, print 0), powers of two (exactly 1), and 30, which is 11110 in binary with four set bits.
hints: Count the 1s in the binary form of n, for example 10 is 1010 in binary and has two of them; 0 has none.
You can test the lowest bit with n & 1 and shift right, but there is a neater trick that jumps straight from one set bit to the next.
n & (n - 1) clears exactly the lowest set bit, so repeat it until n becomes 0 and count the steps; the loop runs once per 1 bit and not at all for 0.

problems.editorial: Push every reading into a max heap and print the root. import sys
a = list(map(int, sys.stdin.read().split()))
nodes = []
for value in a:
    if not nodes:
        nodes.append([value, None, None])
        continue
    at = 0
    while nodes[at][0] != value:
        side = 1 if value < nodes[at][0] else 2
        if nodes[at][side] is None:
            nodes[at][side] = len(nodes)
            nodes.append([value, None, None])
            break
        at = nodes[at][side]
stack = [(0, 1)]
height = 0
while stack:
    at, depth = stack.pop()
    height = max(height, depth)
    for child in nodes[at][1:]:
        if child is not None:
            stack.append((child, depth + 1))
print(height)

problems.title: Connected study groups
problems.description: The input begins n m, followed by m undirected edges u v. Print the number of connected components, including isolated vertices.
problems.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100; 0 ≤ m ≤ 1000; vertex identifiers are 0..n-1. Self loops and parallel edges are allowed.
problems.inputFormat: Read one line.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Start with n components, one per vertex, and process edges with a disjoint-set union. For edge u v, find the root of each endpoint; if the roots differ, link one under the other and decrease the component count, otherwise the edge is redundant. The invariant is that after each edge the count equals the number of distinct roots, which is the number of connected components of the edges seen so far. With path compression and union by size this is nearly O(n + m) time and O(n) space. A BFS or DFS over an adjacency list is an equally valid O(n + m) alternative. Edge cases: m = 0 gives n, self loops and parallel edges never merge anything, and vertices with no edges are components on their own.
hints: Every vertex starts as its own group, and each edge can merge at most two groups into one. Isolated vertices still count.
A disjoint-set union (union-find) tracks which group each vertex belongs to via a representative root.

Start with n components; for each edge, find both roots and, only if they differ, union them and subtract one. Self loops and parallel edges join a vertex to its own group, so they must not decrease the count.

import sys

numbers = [int(token) for token in sys.stdin.read().split()]
n = numbers[0]
parent = list(range(n))


def find(v):
    while parent[v] != v:
        parent[v] = parent[parent[v]]  # path halving keeps trees shallow
        v = parent[v]
    return v


components = n
for i in range(2, len(numbers), 2):
    root_u, root_v = find(numbers[i]), find(numbers[i + 1])
    if root_u != root_v:
        parent[root_u] = root_v
        components -= 1
print(components)

problems.title: Dependency order
problems.description: The input begins n m, followed by m directed dependencies u v (u before v). Print the lexicographically smallest topological order, or CYCLE if no ordering exists.
problems.constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 100; 0 ≤ m ≤ 1000; vertex identifiers are 0..n-1. Self loops and parallel edges are allowed.
problems.inputFormat: Read one line.
problems.outputFormat: Print the requested result. Separate sequence elements with spaces.
problems.editorial: Use Kahn's algorithm with a min-priority queue. Count in-degrees, put every vertex with in-degree 0 in a min-heap, then repeatedly remove the smallest, append it to the order and decrement the in-degree of each successor, pushing those that reach 0. Greedy choice is safe: the smallest ready vertex can go first in some valid order, and putting any larger vertex first would make the sequence lexicographically bigger. If the order ends with fewer than n vertices, the rest lie on or behind a cycle, so print CYCLE. Time is O((n + m) log n) and space O(n + m). Edge cases: isolated vertices, parallel edges (each adds to the in-degree), and self loops, which always mean CYCLE.
hints: A vertex may be printed only after everything that must come before it; if some vertices can never become free, there is a cycle and the answer is CYCLE.
Track each vertex's in-degree, the number of unprinted prerequisites. Vertices with in-degree 0 are ready, and to be lexicographically smallest you must always print the smallest ready vertex.

Run Kahn's algorithm with a min-heap: pop the smallest ready vertex, decrement its successors (once per parallel edge) and push any that reach 0. A self loop never reaches 0, so fewer than n printed vertices means CYCLE.

references.python:
import sys
import heapq

numbers = [int(token) for token in sys.stdin.read().split()]
n = numbers[0]
graph = [[] for _ in range(n)]
indegree = [0] * n
for i in range(2, len(numbers), 2):
    u, v = numbers[i], numbers[i + 1]
    graph[u].append(v)  # parallel edges are kept, so they are also removed one at a time
    indegree[v] += 1

ready = [v for v in range(n) if indegree[v] == 0]
heapq.heapify(ready)
order = []
while ready:
    u = heapq.heappop(ready)  # always take the smallest available vertex
    order.append(u)
    for v in graph[u]:
        indegree[v] -= 1
        if indegree[v] == 0:
            heapq.heappush(ready, v)

if len(order) != n:
    print('CYCLE')
else:
    print(' '.join(str(v) for v in order))
